structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: An outline of the ING Group Annual Report 2024 Sustainability Statement, detailing: general information and basis for preparation; the business model, strategy, and sustainability governance; environmental topics including E1 Climate change (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; transition plan; policies, actions, and performance) and E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; nature strategy; policies, actions, and performance); coverage of the EU Taxonomy regulation; social topics including S1 Own workforce (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; strategy to unlock people’s full potential; policies, actions, and performance) and S4 Consumers and end-users (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; strategy for superior customer value; policies, actions, and performance); and governance through G1 Business conduct (identified impacts, risks and opportunities; policies, actions, and performance). It also shows where the Sustainability Statement sits within the broader annual report, alongside sections such as strategy, financial and risk management, leadership and governance, and financial statements.

structure.title: General information
structure.heading: 1 General information
structure.start_phrase: This report represents our first Sustainability Statement in accordance with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), which we voluntary apply as the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) has not yet been transposed into Dutch law.
structure.summary:
- First Sustainability Statement aligned with ESRS, applied voluntarily as CSRD is not yet transposed into Dutch law.
- Acknowledges market-wide challenges: data availability and reliability, lack of industry-specific guidance, and comparability issues.
- Basis for preparation: covers ING Groep N.V. and subsidiaries (ING Group) for the year ended 31 December 2024, consistent with financial statement consolidation.
- Prepared in line with ESRS and a double materiality assessment (DMA) following EFRAG guidance, covering own operations and the full value chain.
- DMA outcomes define material topics and related impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs), disclosed across Environment, Social, and Governance sections.
- Includes an EU Taxonomy summary in the Environment section and mandatory tables in the Appendix to the Executive Board report.
- Highlights uncertainties: new regulatory implementation, evolving guidance, no industry-specific standard, absence of comparative figures, and the need to embed sustainability into processes and internal controls.
- Data limitations and reliance on estimates: extensive use of external data vendors for emissions and ESG data; vendor processes generally unaudited; ING performs its own data quality reviews but notes residual risk of inaccuracies; plans to refine metrics as better data emerge (details per metric in the Appendix).
- Connectivity with financial statements: monetary amounts for financed emissions, intensity metrics, and transition/physical risks derived from the credit risk portfolio; some disclosures include uncommitted limits; reporting follows internal data standards.
- Transition risk provisioning updated via a management adjustment to capture expected credit losses in the current business lending portfolio.
- Provides navigation to broader report sections (strategy, governance, risk management, financial statements, and appendices).

structure.title: Business model and strategy
structure.heading: 2 Business model and strategy
structure.start_phrase: Our strategy is about growing the difference by providing superior value for our customers and putting sustainability at the heart of what we do.
structure.summary:
- States ING’s strategy to “grow the difference” by delivering superior customer value with sustainability at the core.
- Explains the section’s purpose: to outline material impacts, risks and opportunities, how they link to the strategy and business model, and to provide insights into the Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) methodology.
- Defines the value chain scope for the DMA, extending beyond financial consolidation to include own operations and upstream/downstream relationships; six value-chain segments are identified using internal data.
- Highlights the loan book as the primary channel of sustainability impact; assessments focus on tier 1 direct counterparties, with exceptions for S2 (workers in the value chain) and S4 (consumers/end-users) where tier 2 effects are considered.
- Clarifies that non-consolidated associates and joint ventures are treated as other business relationships within the DMA, while intercompany transactions are excluded.
- Maps key activities, products, services, and actors across the value chain:
  - Upstream: supplier, employee, and property management.
  - Own operations (Retail, Wholesale/Business, Private Banking): lending, payments and cash management, trade finance, deposits and savings, product development, marketing, and distribution of lending, insurance, investment and financial market products.
  - Treasury and investments: high-quality liquid assets, hedging, debt instruments, shareholder’s equity, and equity holdings/investee companies.
  - Downstream actors: large corporates (incl. financial institutions), sovereigns and agencies, SMEs and mid-corporates, self-employed/micro, private individuals, and private banking clients.
- Provides cross-references to related sections (“ING at a glance” and “Strategy, business model and value creation”) for further context.

nodes.title: Business model and strategy - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2 Business model and strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Our strategy is about growing the difference by providing superior value for our customers and putting sustainability at the heart of what we do.
nodes.summary:
Business model and strategy
Our strategy is about growing the difference by providing superior value for our customers and putting 
sustainability at the heart of what we do. With our business we provide services to our Retail  and Wholesale 
clients, worldwide.  For more information on our  operating environment and strategy, see sections ‘ ING at a 
glance ’ and  ‘Strategy, business model and value creation ’. This section provides an overview of our identified 
material impacts, risks and opportunities, how these interact with our strategy and business model, and 
insights into the methodology of our DMA.

nodes.title: Our value chain
nodes.heading: 2.1 Our value chain
nodes.start_phrase: With a view to comprehensively captur e impacts, risks and opportunities, the DMA has to focus on the most significant activities, services and products.
nodes.summary:
- Strategic focus: grow by delivering superior customer value with sustainability embedded at the core; services span Retail and Wholesale clients worldwide.
- Purpose of the section: overview of identified material impacts, risks and opportunities, how they link to strategy and the business model, and an explanation of the Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) methodology; references to related report sections for broader context.
- Value chain approach: DMA targets the most significant activities, products and services; scope extends beyond financial-statement consolidation to include own operations and indirect upstream/downstream relationships; six value-chain segments identified using internal data.
- Key sustainability nexus: the loan book is the primary driver of sustainability impacts; assessments are mainly at tier‑1 direct counterparties (e.g., financed corporates, retail clients), with tier‑2 considered for S2 (workers in the value chain) and S4 (consumers/end-users).
- Boundary choices: non-consolidated associates and joint ventures are treated as other business relationships and included in the DMA; intercompany transactions are excluded.
- Mapped value chain activities: 
  - Wholesale/Business/Retail Banking and Private Individuals: lending, deposits/savings, daily banking, trade finance, capital markets advisory, trading book, mortgages, insurance, investment and wealth-management products; product development, marketing, and distribution.
  - Own operations: supplier management, employee management, property management.
  - Treasury and investments: High Quality Liquid Assets, hedging, debt instruments, shareholder equity, and equity holdings.
- Principal actors covered: suppliers, employees, large corporates (incl. financial institutions), sovereigns/sub-sovereigns/agencies, self-employed/micro firms, SMEs/mid-corporates, private individual and private banking clients, corporate clients, and investee companies.
- Report context: excerpt from ING Group Annual Report 2024, Business model and strategy section.

nodes.title: Our double materiality assessment
nodes.heading: 2.2 Our double materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: This is the first year that we have performed our double materiality assessment in accordance with ESRS, based on the six identified value chain segments.
nodes.summary:
- First ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment, transitioning from prior GRI-based approach; key change is adding financial materiality to impact materiality.
- Materiality definitions:
  - Impact materiality (inside-out): actual or potential positive/negative impacts on people and the environment from financed activities, ING’s own operations, products, services, and business relationships.
  - Financial materiality (outside-in): risks and opportunities from environmental and societal changes affecting ING, notably via climate and environmental risk management.
- Time horizons used: very short (<1 year), short (1–3 years), medium (3–5 years), long (>5 years and at least 10), with ESRS requiring some forward-looking disclosures.
- Scope and evaluation: DMA based on six value chain segments; covers sector-agnostic topics E1–E5 (climate, pollution, water/marine resources, biodiversity/ecosystems, resource use/circular economy), S1–S4 (own workforce, workers in the value chain, affected communities, consumers/end-users), and G1 (business conduct), assessed for risk, opportunity, and double materiality with thresholds (Material, Important, Informative–Minimal).
- Outcomes: Despite methodology shift, topic-level results broadly consistent with prior year. S2 (Workers in the value chain) and S3 (Affected communities) not deemed material for ING’s value chains but still considered important.
- Salient human rights issues:
  - As lender to corporates: forced labour, child labour, land and resource-related community issues.
  - As procurer: occupational health and safety, modern slavery and forced labour.
  - Identification, management, and mitigation detailed in ING’s latest human rights report (ing.com).

nodes.title: Process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 2.3 Process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: Via the double materiality assessment process, ING identifies impacts, risk s and opportunities across environmental, social and governance (ESG) sustainability matters, arising from its own operations or within the upstream or downstream value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Explains ING’s process for identifying impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) across its operations and value chain using a Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) aligned with ESRS.
- DMA governance and flow: Five-step approach—(1) identify activities and business relationships, (2) identify relevant sustainability matters, (3) execute the DMA, (4) validate results through stakeholder engagement, (5) obtain Management Board and Supervisory Board approval.
- Scoping methodology: Starts from balance sheet and P&L to pinpoint activities/assets subject to IROs; maps financial statement items to core business areas and portfolios; excludes portfolios with low likelihood of material IROs.
- Exposure classification: Categorizes assets and liabilities by characteristics such as loan/position maturity, counterparty type, product/service type, geography, industry, and collateral to understand where sustainability issues can materialize.
- Sustainability matters selection: Uses ESRS sector-agnostic inventory as the baseline for alignment and comparability; conducts market consultation and reviews past assessments to find entity-specific topics—none added; assesses topics across the full value chain, recognizing relevance varies by chain (details in the appendix).
- Assessment granularity: Evaluates all ESRS topics at sub-topic level; Social matters assessed at sub-sub-topic level; granularity set by internal and external data availability.
- Impact drivers: Defines and considers environmental (e.g., resource use, emissions), social (e.g., labor practices, human rights, equity, community health/safety), and governance (e.g., transparency, accountability, anti-corruption, compliance) drivers, with a forward-looking perspective.
- Risk drivers: Identifies ESG risks within existing risk categories, including transition and physical risks; accounts for forward-looking characteristics and dependencies on natural and human capital; links to broader ESG risk management.
- Opportunity drivers: Views opportunities as ESG-related conditions that can enhance the business model, strategy delivery, and value creation; prioritization aligned with publicly disclosed sustainability commitments.

nodes.title: Execution of the double materiality assessment
nodes.heading: 2.4 Execution of the double materiality assessment
nodes.start_phrase: The DMA leverages on renowned external data sources , internal data, voluntary reports and other regulatory disclosures to assess the impact from ING’s own operations and upstream and downstream value chain .
nodes.summary:
- Explains how ING executes its Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) across its full value chain (own operations, upstream, downstream) using a “gross” approach that excludes mitigating actions.
- Identifies data foundations: renowned external sources, internal data, voluntary reports, and regulatory disclosures; combines quantitative and qualitative methods against predefined thresholds.
- Defines impact materiality via severity (scale, scope, irremediability) and likelihood across time horizons for both actual and potential positive/negative impacts.
- Defines financial materiality via magnitude and likelihood arising from impacts, dependencies, and context analyses; considers dependencies on natural, human, and social resources, business relationships, and reputation; supplements indicators with expert judgment.
- Details risk assessment: mirrors approach for negative impacts and dependencies; incorporates individual exposures and context; determines portfolio risk materiality as the maximum across dimensions; enhanced by internal data and scenario analyses.
- Details opportunity assessment: evaluates magnitude (financial and non-financial gains, e.g., cost savings) across “use of own resources” and “reliance on relationships” dimensions; likelihood tied to time horizon.
- Describes scoring framework: combined scores from 1 (minimal) to 5 (critical) using a conversion matrix of severity/magnitude versus likelihood; sustainability matters are material if rated “critical” or “significant.”
- References “Technical notes to the double materiality assessment” for further methodological details and value-chain-specific sustainability matters.

nodes.title: Validation of the outcome through stakeholders’ engagement
nodes.heading: 2.5 Validation of the outcome through stakeholders’ engagement
nodes.start_phrase: To validate the outcome of our double materiality assessment, we engaged with our key stakeholders.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines how ING validated the results of its double materiality assessment (DMA) through structured engagement with two stakeholder groups—affected stakeholders and users. It describes a standardized process of workshops, surveys, and in-depth interviews to review the DMA methodology, preliminary results, completeness, and different time horizons, with interview minutes confirmed to ensure accuracy. Where direct engagement was not feasible, proxies were used (e.g., NGOs for affected communities and nature; internal and public data for retail customers). Stakeholder feedback was evaluated systematically for recurrence, consistency, evidentiary support, and relevance, with references cross-checked and discussed with subject-matter experts. An example is provided where some stakeholders expected “Workers in the value chain (S2)” and “Affected communities (S3)” to be material; ING maintained their non-material status given limited portfolio exposure to high human-rights-risk sectors, while continuing to report on them as salient human rights issues. The text also details stakeholder-specific engagement channels and focus areas: employees (S1, G1), customers and investors (all ESRS topics), and society via NGOs and regulatory experts (E1–E5, S2–S4, and all ESRS topics for governments/regulators). Finally, it records governance approvals: methodology endorsed by the ESG Risk Committee and the DMA outcome approved by the management boards and Supervisory Board, following communication to internal stakeholders and value-chain owners.

nodes.title: Approval by the management boards and Supervisory Board
nodes.heading: 2.6 Approval by the management boards and Supervisory Board
nodes.start_phrase: The outcome of the DMA was communicated to all relevant stakeholders and value-chain segment owners.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Validate the double materiality assessment (DMA) outcomes and identified material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) with stakeholders, checking recognition and any missing topics.
- Stakeholder scope and methods: Two groups—affected stakeholders and users—engaged via sessions, surveys, and in-depth interviews. A standardized approach covered soundness, completeness, and different time horizons. Interview minutes were confirmed to ensure accurate interpretation.
- Use of proxies: NGOs represented affected communities and silent stakeholders such as nature and biodiversity; internal and public data represented private customers; ING experts covered supervisory/public/regulatory perspectives when direct engagement was not possible.
- Feedback evaluation: Inputs were analyzed for recurrence, consistency, strength, evidence, and relevance; patterns across groups were identified; fact-based substantiation was prioritized and cross-checked with credible sources and subject-matter experts.
- Example outcome: Despite some stakeholder expectations for Workers in the value chain (S2) and Affected communities (S3) to be material, ING maintained its DMA outcome due to limited exposure to human rights–vulnerable sectors, while continuing to report on these salient issues in the human rights report.
- Governance and approvals: DMA methodology approved by the ESG Risk Committee; outcomes approved by the management boards and the Supervisory Board, after communication to relevant stakeholders and value-chain owners.
- Engagement by stakeholder segment:
  - Our people: Direct workshops with employees; proxies via European/local works councils; feedback via surveys and interviews; focus on S1 and G1.
  - Our customers: Retail via proxies (customer complaints, consumer protection publications); Business and Wholesale via proxies (sessions with ING sector experts); focus on all ESRS topics.
  - Investors: Direct sessions with investors and associations; focus on all ESRS topics.
  - Society: Direct sessions with NGOs as proxies for nature, biodiversity, climate, and workers in the value chain; proxy sessions with ING regulatory/public affairs experts; focus on E1–E5, S2–S4, and all ESRS topics for governments and regulators.

nodes.title: Reporting on the material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 2.7 Reporting on the material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: For each material sustainability matter, ING reviewed the associated disclosure and application requirements included in the ESRSs.
nodes.summary:
- Describes ING’s approach to reporting material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities under ESRS for the 2024 Sustainability Statement.
- States that ING disclosed applicable mandatory, relevant, and material information, while omitting certain requirements not applicable in the initial years; details are in the Reference index.
- Explains integration of sustainability risk management and internal controls into ING’s ERM framework and three-lines-of-defence model to strengthen governance and align with financial and non-financial oversight.
- Notes that the CSRD sustainability statement preparation is aligned with ING’s annual integrated reporting process and governance.
- Acknowledges inherent risks of material misstatement (e.g., human error, third-party controls, fraud) and indicates mitigating measures have been implemented.
- Provides cross-references to the Risk management framework and the Reference index within the ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Internal controls over sustainability reporting
nodes.heading: 2.8 Internal controls over sustainability reporting
nodes.start_phrase: At ING we have integrated our sustainability-related risk management and internal controls into our existing Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework and three-lines-of-defence model.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and standards: ING reports on material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) in line with ESRS disclosure and application requirements. For the 2024 Sustainability Statement, ING includes applicable mandatory, relevant and material information, while omitting certain requirements not applicable in the first reporting years. A Reference index provides details.

- Governance and controls: Sustainability-related risk management and internal controls are integrated into ING’s Enterprise Risk Management framework and three-lines-of-defence model, aligned with the annual integrated reporting and CSRD governance. ING acknowledges risk of material misstatement (e.g., human error, third-party controls, fraud) and has implemented mitigating measures.

- IRO overview table: Presents where IROs arise across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream), the time horizons (very short to long term), and which business models are affected (Private Individuals, Private Banking, Wholesale Banking, Business Banking).

- Environmental
  - Climate change (E1)
    - Negative impact: financing high-emitting sectors and non–energy-efficient properties.
    - Risks: potential (non)financial losses from transition risks (defaults, reduced collateral values) and physical risks (storms, floods, sea-level rise, temperature increases).
    - Opportunities: ING’s voluntary commitments to support clients’ climate transition.
    - Broadly spans the value chain, multiple time horizons; affects Private Individuals, Private Banking, Wholesale Banking, Business Banking.
  - Biodiversity (E4)
    - Negative impact: lending to clients whose operations cause irreversible harm to species.
    - Risks: reputational and financial losses tied to severity of impacts.
    - Primarily linked to Wholesale Banking.

- Social
  - Own workforce (S1)
    - Negative impacts: unrealistic workloads, gender inequality, pay gaps, inadequate prevention of violence and harassment—affecting wellbeing, especially for vulnerable groups.
    - Positive impacts: upskilling, new competencies, diverse teams.
    - Risks: reputational and turnover risks; risks related to disability inclusion and workplace accessibility.
    - Located in own operations; relevant across time horizons.
  - Consumers and end-users (S4)
    - Negative impacts: insufficient access to quality information, lack of social inclusion, inadequate privacy protection—potentially harming customer wellbeing.
    - Risks: financial losses, regulatory exposure, reputational harm.
    - Applies to Private Individuals and Private Banking; primarily downstream; spans multiple time horizons.

- Governance
  - Business conduct (G1)
    - Risks: financial loss, regulatory fines, and reputational damage from breaches of corporate culture, bribery and corruption, and failure to protect whistleblowers.
    - Located in own operations; relevant across time horizons.

structure.title: Our sustainability governance
structure.heading: 3 Our sustainability governance
structure.start_phrase: At ING, we have integrated sustainability into our existing governance.
structure.summary:
- ING integrates sustainability into its existing governance framework; detailed roles and composition of the Supervisory Board (SB), Executive Board (EB), and Management Board Banking (MBB) are covered elsewhere, while this section focuses on sustainability governance.
- Supervisory Board: An ad hoc ESG Committee created in 2022 became a permanent committee in 2024. It meets quarterly, includes at least one member from each other SB committee, and is combined with the Audit Committee when disclosure or control topics are on the agenda. nodes.title: Climate change - Introduction
nodes.heading: 4.1 Climate change
nodes.start_phrase: Our climate is changing due to the release of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions into the atmosphere.
nodes.summary:
Climate change
Our climate is changing due to the release of greenhouse gas  (GHG) emissions into the atmosphere. Our 
climate action activities are focused on the three areas where we believe we can make the greatest impact: 
helping to drive down emissions to meet the global goal of net zero by 2050; building up the financing of the 
new technologies and sustainable systems of the future; and finding ways to enable people to play their part 
in the transition. For ING, climate adaptation is essential to reduce vulnerability against the physical impact 
of climate change. We work on reducing those risks by financing the required adaptation of our clients and 
communities . 
Identified  impacts, risks and opportuniti es

nodes.title: Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 4.1.1 Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: This section elaborates on the material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) associated with climate change, and how these factors interact with and influence ING’s strategy and business model.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and goals: ING addresses climate change by targeting three impact areas—reducing emissions to align with net zero by 2050, scaling finance for new low‑carbon technologies and sustainable systems, and enabling people to contribute to the transition—while emphasizing climate adaptation to lower vulnerability to physical climate impacts by financing client and community resilience measures.

- Material IROs and scope: Climate change mitigation and adaptation are deemed material across Wholesale Banking (WB), Business Banking (BB), and Private Individuals (PI) real estate lending. A sector transition plan prioritizes the most carbon‑intensive sectors and is complemented by policies and guidelines that manage negative impacts, risks, and create opportunities.

- Mitigation: 
  - Negative impacts: Emissions linked to lending in high‑emitting sectors; and, in real estate, properties with poor energy performance, assessed using the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD).
  - Risks (transition risk): For WB/BB, costs from adopting low‑carbon technologies and exposure to carbon pricing (including indirect emissions); for real estate, energy price changes and EPBD IV effects on customer income, repayment capacity, and renovation financing eligibility. Non‑compliance can lead to reputational, legal/regulatory, and financial consequences.
  - Opportunities: Growth aligned with public commitments—mobilizing more WB volumes for the transition, issuing green funding, and advancing the Terra approach via increased renewable financing.

- Adaptation:
  - Definition and linkage: Adjusting to actual/anticipated climate impacts; closely tied to managing physical risk.
  - Physical risks: Acute (storms, floods) and chronic (rising sea levels and temperatures) hazards that heighten default risk and non‑performing loans through multiple transmission channels, creating financial vulnerabilities for ING.

nodes.title: Climate change mitigation
nodes.heading: 4.1.2 Climate change mitigation
nodes.start_phrase: Climate change mitigation refers to the process of reducing GHG emissions and holding the increase in the global average temperature to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels, in line with the ambition of the Paris Agreement1.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: ING’s climate strategy centers on mitigating and adapting to climate change across Wholesale Banking, Business Banking, and Private Individuals (real estate lending), with a goal aligned to net zero by 2050.
- Three climate action pillars: 1) drive down emissions, 2) finance new low‑carbon technologies and sustainable systems, and 3) enable people to participate in the transition; adaptation financing is emphasized to reduce physical climate vulnerability.
- Management approach: A sector transition plan targets the most carbon‑intensive sectors, complemented by policies and guidelines that address negative impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Mitigation: Defined as reducing GHG emissions to limit warming to 1.5°C (Paris Agreement). Key negative impacts arise from lending to high‑emitting sectors and to real estate with poor energy performance (assessed against EPBD).
- Transition risks: For corporates, costs of new technologies/retrofits and carbon pricing on indirect emissions; for real estate, energy price changes and EPBD IV effects on income, payment behavior, and renovation financing eligibility; plus compliance risks (reputational, legal/regulatory, financial).
- Opportunities: Scaling climate transition financing via increased Wholesale Banking volumes mobilised, green funding frameworks, the Terra approach, and expanded renewable financing ambitions.
- Adaptation and physical risk: Defined as adjusting to actual/expected impacts; physical risks stem from acute events (storms, floods) and chronic trends (sea-level rise, temperature increases), raising default and non-performing loan risks through multiple transmission channels.
- Materiality: Climate mitigation and adaptation are material topics across ING’s key value chains and influence strategy and the business model.

nodes.title: Climate change adaptation
nodes.heading: 4.1.3 Climate change adaptation
nodes.start_phrase: Climate change adaptation refers to the process of adjusting to actual and anticipated climate change and its impacts.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and strategy: ING targets three climate action priorities—driving emissions down toward net zero by 2050, scaling financing for new low‑carbon technologies and sustainable systems, and enabling customers to participate in the transition—while prioritizing climate adaptation to reduce vulnerability to physical impacts by financing client and community resilience.
- Scope of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs): Climate change mitigation and adaptation are material across Wholesale Banking (WB), Business Banking (BB), and Private Individuals (PI; real estate lending). ING manages IROs via a sector transition plan for carbon‑intensive sectors, complemented by policies and guidelines that address both risks and opportunities.
- Mitigation—negative impacts: Lending to high‑emitting sectors and to low‑efficiency real estate increases GHG emissions and long‑term temperature rise risk; poor energy performance properties are high impact in the short/medium term and all non‑net‑zero properties in the long term (assessed via EPBD).
- Mitigation—risks: Transition risk for corporates arises from decarbonization costs (technology upgrades, retrofits, indirect supplier costs) and carbon pricing; for real estate, energy price changes and EPBD IV implementation may strain borrower income, payment behavior, and renovation financing eligibility. Non‑compliance may trigger reputational, legal, regulatory, and financial consequences.
- Mitigation—opportunities: ING aims to expand sustainable finance through increased WB mobilized volumes, green funding frameworks, the Terra approach, and renewable financing ambitions.
- Adaptation—physical risks: Acute events (storms, floods) and chronic shifts (sea level rise, temperature increases) can cause defaults and losses.
  - Residential real estate: Asset damage, devaluations, insurance availability constraints, and borrower income impairment after disasters.
  - Wholesale/Business Banking: Infrastructure damage, operational interruptions, cost increases, revenue declines, supply disruptions, higher insurance costs, and third‑party claims affect borrower profitability and repayment capacity.
  - Governments/sovereigns: Lower tax revenues and higher spending for disaster response/adaptation can raise borrowing costs and restrict market access.
- Financial effects and resilience:
  - Current effects: Climate risk not yet fully embedded in IFRS 9 ECL due to data gaps; 2024 steps include explicit climate risk drivers in provisioning. Physical risk effects are based on actual events (e.g., Spain provision for payment holidays after Valencia floods). Transition risk captured via a management adjustment to ECL for current corporate portfolios.
  - Anticipated effects: Disclosures aligned with phased‑in EBA Pillar III ESG templates—Template 5 (physical risk exposures) and Template 2 (real estate energy efficiency)—with scope and resilience analysis in the appendix.
  - Risk controls: For material physical risks, mandatory credit risk mitigations (insurance or alternatives), enhanced underwriting data on adaptation, controlled financing amounts, or asset rejection if unmitigated; real estate valuations must reflect jurisdiction‑specific hazards.
- View on transition risk and stranded assets: High‑emitting sector exposure does not automatically imply default; structured transition planning and robust risk management can enable viable transformation. A three‑year horizon is too short to attribute defaults solely to transition failure; classifying all high‑carbon exposures as stranded over longer horizons is overly conservative. Bottom‑up transition risk assessment remains challenging due to data and forecasting limits.
- Real estate transition uncertainty: EPBD IV transposition into national law is expected by May 2026, creating interim uncertainty in linking EPC/primary energy demand to transition risk; sector transition plans for commercial and residential real estate are in place.
- Overall coverage: ING considers mid‑term transition risk significantly addressed through its Terra approach, which covers most emissions‑intensive sectors in the WB loan book.

nodes.title: Financial effects and resilience of ING’s strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 4.1.4 Financial effects and resilience of ING’s strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: For the identified risks we have two approaches to determine our current financial effects, more explicitly for physical risk and transition risk.
nodes.summary:
- Physical risk impacts by segment:
  - Residential real estate: extreme events can cause write-offs, asset devaluations, early retirements, reduced insurance availability; borrower distress may impair loan servicing and renovation financing.
  - Wholesale/Business Banking: infrastructure damage, operational interruptions, higher costs, reduced demand, supply issues, facility damage, third-party claims, and rising insurance premiums can depress income and increase default risk.
  - Governments: lower tax revenues and higher spending from disaster response/adaptation may raise borrowing costs or restrict market access.

- Financial effects and resilience:
  - Two approaches to quantify climate impacts: event-based provisioning for physical risk and a management adjustment for transition-risk ECLs.
  - IFRS 9 ECL models cannot yet fully isolate climate risk due to limited data, though 2024 enhancements add climate-risk drivers.
  - Example: 2024 provision in Spain for payment holidays after severe floods in Valencia.
  - Disclosures follow phased EBA Pillar III ESG: Template 5 (physical risk exposures) and Template 2 (real estate energy efficiency).
  - Proactive risk management: mandatory mitigations (insurance/adaptation), enhanced underwriting data, controlled financing, or asset rejection; material hazards embedded in real estate valuations.

- Transition risk perspective:
  - Arises from policy, technology, and market shifts; high-emitting sectors face capex and indirect supplier costs, and potential demand decline.
  - Not all high-emitting sectors will default; caution against labeling all exposures as stranded, especially over short horizons; bottom-up assessments remain challenging.
  - Real estate efficiency upgrades are a component of transition risk, with regulatory uncertainty pending EPBD IV transposition (expected May 2026).
  - Mid-term transition risk largely addressed via the Terra approach across emissions-intense sectors.

- Climate stress testing:
  - ING’s climate stress-test extends existing ICAAP/EBA frameworks with overlays for transition and physical risks on corporate and mortgage credit portfolios.

- Opportunities and commitments:
  - Support clients’ sustainable transition through products and green funding.
  - Financial effects tracked via progress against public commitments (e.g., Terra transition plan for renewable power, mobilized volumes, green funding framework).

- Transition plan and Terra approach:
  - Sustainability is core to strategy; aim to steer the most carbon-intensive portfolio segments toward climate goals.
  - Terra measures client emission intensities against sector decarbonization pathways; upstream oil & gas steered on financial exposure.
  - Collection of Client Transition Plans in Wholesale Banking to deepen sector plans and guide client engagement, advisory, and financing.
  - Monitoring absolute financed emissions enables hotspot analyses and informs expansion of the Terra scope.

nodes.title: Our transition plan
nodes.heading: 4.1.5 Our transition plan
nodes.start_phrase: At ING, putting sustainability at the heart of what we do is one of the core pillars of our strategy.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines ING’s climate and sustainability approach within its 2024 Annual Report. It highlights enhancements to a dedicated climate stress-testing methodology—built on ICAAP/EBA frameworks—that assesses transition and physical climate risks on corporate and mortgage credit exposures. ING emphasizes supporting clients’ low‑carbon transitions through green products and funding, tracking progress via publicly disclosed commitments rather than direct financial effects. Central to its strategy is the Terra transition plan: measuring emission intensities in the most carbon‑intensive sectors (steering upstream oil & gas by financial exposure), benchmarking against sector decarbonisation scenarios, and integrating Client Transition Plan (CTP) assessments in Wholesale Banking. ING uses these insights to engage clients, steer its lending portfolio, finance transition solutions, measure absolute financed emissions where possible, conduct hotspot analyses, and expand the Terra scope to manage risks and identify opportunities.

nodes.summary:
Our Terra approach  
ING’s integrated climate approach considers how we can mitigate climate change through our lending 
activities as well as how climate change may adversely impact our business. Our Terra approach is based on 
three main principles: (1) impact-based, (2) climate science-based, (3) engagement-driven. Our transition 
plan, guided by our Terra approach, is portfolio- and sector-focused. It measures how our most carbon-
intensive clients have progressed against their sector net-zero pathways, as well as the progress in net-zero 
alignment of our portfolio on a sector and portfolio level. This approach allows us to set decarbonisation 
targets and identify the corresponding actions for each sector to manage the transition risks of our balance 
sheet. For details about the process of identifying our transition risks and the corresponding policies, see the 
‘Policies, actions and performance ’ section.

nodes.title: Target setting and portfolio steering
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.1 Target setting and portfolio steering
nodes.start_phrase: We use financed emissions as a hotspot analysis to prioritise high-emitting sectors, after which we select the science-based scenario.
nodes.summary:
- Describes ING’s Terra approach as the bank’s integrated climate strategy for both mitigating climate change through lending and managing climate-related risks to its business.

- Details target-setting and portfolio steering: using financed emissions for hotspot analysis to prioritize high‑emitting sectors, selecting science-based scenarios, and focusing on the most impactful parts of value chains.
- Notes targets are based on methodologies developed with peers and experts, including defining which products are in scope.

nodes.title: Scenario selection, target setting and metrics measurement
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.2 Scenario selection, target setting and metrics measurement
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the selection process, and to align our lending portfolio with net zero, we check whether there is an available International Energy Agency (IEA) NZE scenario or other relevant scientific 1.5°C scenarios from recognised institutions.
nodes.summary:
- Uses recognized 1.5°C scenarios—preferably IEA Net Zero Emissions (NZE)—to set sector-specific net‑zero targets, always applying the most recent scenarios.
- Keeps reporting boundaries consistent between baseline and reporting years; sector coverage is defined by adopted methodologies and available scientific scenarios.
- Translates sector benchmark scenarios into convergence pathways for ING’s portfolio, with intermediary 2030 targets that align toward net zero by 2050.
- Calculates alignment metrics using latest available emissions data (generally 2023, from external providers) and financial data as of year-end 2024; for shipping and aviation, both emissions and financial data use year-end 2023 to align reporting periods.
- Does not use offsets—now or in future—for Terra targets; external data providers also exclude offsets when assessing clients’ climate performance.
- Notes that targets, baselines, methodologies, and approach may evolve due to international agreements, regulation, data quality/availability, pathway updates, public policy, and sector/client developments.
- Steers the loan portfolio primarily on emissions intensity or alignment delta by sector (exception: upstream oil & gas is steered on financial exposure).
- Explains why financed emissions are not used for steering: while useful for hotspot analysis, they rely on multiple assumptions and mainly drive divestment-based action; intensity metrics better support client engagement and real-economy transition.
- Clarifies that, in a hypothetical scenario with all assumptions fixed, financed emissions would move with intensity, but real-world variability makes intensity a more effective steering metric.
- Distinguishes between Terra intensity metrics and financed emissions: different product scopes and sector focus; Terra targets specific sectors and high-emitting clients, whereas financed emissions include on‑balance sheet term loans, revolvers, and leases per PCAF.
- References further detail in “Technical notes to the sector transition plan” and situates the content within the Environment section of ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.start_phrase: As part of the selection process, and to align our lending portfolio with net zero, we check whether there is an available International Energy Agency (IEA) NZE scenario or other relevant scientific 1.5°C scenarios from recognised institutions.
nodes.summary: Introduces ING’s approach to scenario selection, target setting, and metrics measurement for aligning its lending portfolio with net zero, using the most recent IEA NZE or other recognized 1.5°C scientific scenarios to set sector-specific targets. Reporting boundaries keep emissions scopes consistent between baseline and reporting years, with sector coverage defined by adopted methodologies and scenarios. Benchmark scenarios are translated into sector convergence pathways that inform 2030 intermediary targets and converge to net zero by 2050. Alignment metrics are calculated using latest available emissions data (generally 2023) from external providers against ING’s year-end 2024 financial data; for shipping and aviation, both asset emissions and financial data are aligned to year-end 2023. Offsets are not used or planned in the Terra approach, and data providers also exclude client offsets. nodes.title: We steer our portfolio based on emission intensity
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.2.1 We steer our portfolio based on emission intensity
nodes.start_phrase: When setting up the transition plans in scope of our Terra approach, we apply what we consider to be the best-fit methodology for each sector to measure and steer our loan book.
nodes.summary:
- Scenario basis: Targets are set using the most recent IEA Net Zero Emissions (NZE) or other recognized 1.5°C scientific scenarios, selected per sector.
- Reporting boundaries: Emissions scopes and sector coverage are consistent between baseline and reporting years, defined by adopted methodologies and available scientific scenarios.
- Convergence pathways: Sector benchmark scenarios are translated into pathways that guide ING’s portfolio alignment, underpinning 2030 intermediary targets and convergence to net zero by 2050.
- Data and timing: Alignment metrics use the latest available emissions data (generally 2023) from external providers and year-end 2024 financial data; shipping and aviation require both emissions and financial data aligned to year-end 2023 due to methodology.
- No offsets: Offsets are not used to measure portfolio alignment or to achieve Terra targets; data providers also exclude offsets in clients’ climate performance.
- Change factors: Commitments, targets, and methodologies may evolve due to international agreements, regulation, data quality/availability, pathway updates, policy changes, and sector or societal developments.
- Steering approach: ING steers its portfolio primarily on emissions intensity or alignment deltas by sector (exception: upstream oil & gas steered on financial exposure), supporting client engagement and transition rather than divestment.
- Financed emissions vs intensity: Financed emissions aid hotspot analysis but are less effective for steering; intensity-based targets avoid heavy reliance on assumptions about future client emissions, valuations, and balance sheet composition.
- Scope differences: Terra intensity metrics cover specific sectors and high-emitting clients with tailored methodologies, while financed emissions (per PCAF) include on-balance lending products such as term loans, revolvers, and leases.

nodes.title: Difference between intensity metrics and financed emissions
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.2.2 Difference between intensity metrics and financed emissions
nodes.start_phrase: As a financial institution, we finance economic activities which we present as our outstandings.
nodes.summary:
- Describes how ING selects climate scenarios and sets targets to align its lending portfolio with net zero, prioritizing IEA NZE and other reputable 1.5°C pathways and using the most recent versions.
- Defines consistent reporting boundaries between baseline and reporting years, with sector coverage determined by adopted methodologies and available scientific scenarios.
- Translates sectoral benchmark scenarios into convergence pathways that set 2030 interim targets and aim for net zero by 2050.
- Calculates alignment metrics using latest available emissions data (generally 2023) against year-end 2024 financials; for shipping and aviation both emissions and financial data are aligned to year-end 2023 due to methodology requirements.
- States no use of carbon offsets—now or in future—for portfolio alignment; data providers also exclude offsets.
- Notes that commitments, targets, and methods may evolve due to changing international agreements, regulation, data quality/availability, policy, and sectoral or societal developments.
- Explains portfolio steering based on emissions intensity or alignment delta (except upstream oil & gas, which is steered on financial exposure), rather than absolute financed emissions.
- Justifies intensity-based steering as more suitable for a bank’s role in financing and client engagement; financed emissions are useful for hotspot analysis but less effective for active portfolio steering without divestment.
- Clarifies that converting intensity targets to financed emissions would require many assumptions; only in a hypothetical steady-state would financed emissions mirror intensity changes.
- Differentiates Terra intensity metrics from financed emissions: different product scopes and a focus on specific high-emitting sectors for Terra, while financed emissions include on-balance sheet term loans, revolvers, and leases per PCAF.

nodes.title: Our sector transition plans
nodes.heading: 4.1.7 Our sector transition plans
nodes.start_phrase: Our Terra toolbox, as shown below, is a summary of our approach per sector.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt outlines ING’s sector transition plans within its Terra approach, explaining that for each key sector it assesses observed challenges, actions needed from society, its performance, and ING’s own actions. Definitions and details are referenced in the Appendix to the Executive Board report.

- A “Terra toolbox” table summarizes, per sector, the in-scope portfolio exposure, methodology used, emissions scopes covered, financial products included, the decarbonization metric, the 2030 scenario/pathway, baseline year and values, 2024 portfolio metric, distance to the IEA 2030 convergence point, the 2030 target versus baseline, and a 1.5°C-aligned reference value for 2050 (where applicable). Notes clarify that negative “distance” values mean performance is already ahead of the 2030 pathway and that real estate uses a whole-building approach including occupant electricity.

- Sectors, methods, metrics, and selected highlights:
  - Power generation (€11.5bn): PACTA; Scope 1; kg CO2e/MWh; IEA NZA (WEO 2023). 2024 is 4% ahead of the IEA 2030 convergence; 2030 intensity target −78% vs baseline; 1.5°C reference −100% by 2040.
  - Oil & gas – Upstream (€1.0bn): PACTA Credit Application and PCAF; Scopes 1–3; outstanding amount and absolute emissions; IEA NZE (WEO 2023). Outstanding down 61% vs baseline; absolute emissions down 78%; 2030 targets −35% (exposure) and −50% (emissions); 1.5°C reference −100% by 2040.
  - Oil & gas – Mid-/Downstream (€7.4bn): Convergence approach; Scopes 1–2; kg CO2e/boe; IEA NZE (2023). Needs 31% reduction to 2030 convergence; 2030 target −24%; 1.5°C −100%.
  - Cement (€0.7bn): PACTA; Scopes 1–2; t CO2/t cement; IEA NZE (2023). 33% above 2030 path; 2030 target −29%; 1.5°C −97%.
  - Steel (€2.0bn): Sustainable STEEL Principles; Scopes 1–2 and part of 3; SSP alignment score and t CO2/t steel; IEA NZE (2021) and MPP Technology Moratorium. 2024 SSP alignment score 0.83 with target 0 by 2030; intensity path indicates a 32% gap to 2030.
  - Automotive (€4.0bn): PACTA; Scope 3 Cat.11; kg CO2/vkm; IEA NZE (2021). 45% above 2030 convergence; 2030 target −49%; 1.5°C −98%.
  - Aviation (€4.1bn): Pegasus Guidelines; Scope 1 and part of 3; g CO2e/RTK; MPP PRU 2023. 33% above 2030 convergence; 2030 target −19%; 1.5°C −100%.
  - Shipping (€8.6bn): Poseidon Principles; Scope 1; alignment delta vs DNV 1.5°C Initiative. 2024 alignment delta −7.6% (ahead of trajectory); target 0% by 2030 and 2050.
  - Commercial real estate (€26.2bn): PCAF/CRREM; Scopes 1–2; kg CO2e/m²; CRREM 1.5°C (IEA NZE-based). 131% above 2030 convergence; 2030 target −56%; 1.5°C −98%.
  - Residential real estate (€294.3bn): PCAF/CRREM; Scopes 1–2; kg CO2e/m²; CRREM 1.5°C. Metrics reported (baseline 2021 and 2024), with distance and targets not specified in this table.

- The section sits within ING Group’s Annual Report 2024 Sustainability Statement (Environment) and signals that subsequent sections provide sector-by-sector overviews of challenges, needed societal actions, ING’s performance, and planned actions.

nodes.title: Power generation
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.1 Power generation
nodes.start_phrase: We expect the power-generation industry to maximise renewable energy and boost power-storage technology.
nodes.summary:
- Sector outlook: Emphasis on maximizing renewable power generation, accelerating power‑storage deployment (batteries, hydrogen) with incentives where needed, enabling carbon capture and storage on waste/biomass incineration to deliver negative emissions, and expanding/modernizing grids to meet rising demand, higher renewable volatility, and extreme weather.
- Emission intensity performance (Terra): Calculated using 2024 portfolio outstanding and 2023 emissions data; improved by 41% from 106 to 63 kg CO2e/MWh (2023 to 2024). 2024 in-scope outstanding: €11.5 billion. ING target: −78% vs 2018 by 2030; distance to 2030 IEA convergence: −4%.
- Steering methodology: ING steers the power portfolio via the Terra approach; financed emissions are reported but not used for sector steering. 2023 emissions data applied as 2024 data is not yet available.
- Financed emissions trend: Scope 1&2 increased by +693 kt CO2e to 11,103 kt; Scope 3 increased by +1,314 kt CO2e to 5,728 kt, driven by portfolio growth and higher drawdowns among some higher‑emitting clients.
- Coal policy and exposure: Since 2015, no financing of new coal‑fired power plants or thermal coal mines. Target set in 2017 to reduce coal‑fired plant financing to near zero by end‑2025. Outstanding to individual coal‑fired plants remains €77 million (legacy loans), with continued reduction efforts.
- Renewable financing commitments: Target tripled in 2023 to €7.5 billion annually by 2025 (from €2.5 billion set in 2022). In 2024, €7 billion of new renewable generation financing committed (mainly wind and solar).
- Transaction highlight: Over €900 million financing to Sosteneo Infrastructure Partners for 49% of Enel Libra Flexsys, comprising 23 battery energy storage projects (1.7 GW) and refurbishment of open-cycle CCGT plants (0.9 GW). Provides critical flexibility and reliability to the Italian grid; revenues contracted for 15 years via capacity agreements with Enel, backed by Terna S.p.A.

nodes.title: Oil & gas
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.2 Oil & gas
nodes.start_phrase: Oil & gas accounts for about 60 percent of all primary energy consumed worldwide1.
nodes.summary:
- Sets global context: Oil and gas provide ~60% of primary energy. In the IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 scenario, combustion of crude oil and natural gas for energy phases out; sustainable bio- and e‑fuels must reach 13% of total energy by 2030. Decarbonisation is required across the mid- and downstream value chain, prioritising methane leak reduction and leveraging carbon capture and storage (CCS).
- Explains ING’s Terra approach, targets and 2024 performance: outstandings to clients in Terra scope fell 13% to €1.001 billion (from €1.155 billion in 2023) due to portfolio composition changes and active steering toward 2030/2040 targets. Emissions intensity improved 1% to 19.1 kg CO2e/boe, calculated using 2022 emissions data pending 2023/2024 availability.
- Upstream oil & gas steering and financed emissions: portfolio is steered on measured outstandings and financed emissions. 2024 financed emissions declined to 702 kt CO2e (Scopes 1–2, down 867 kt) and 10,325 kt CO2e (Scope 3, down 13,343 kt), mainly from portfolio size reduction and lower exposure to higher emitters. Total financed emissions ~11 Mt CO2e; outstanding in scope ~€1.0 billion. Target: −35% vs 2019 by 2030; shown distance to 2030 IEA convergence metric −61%.
- Mid- and downstream oil & gas approach: sector is steered via Terra emissions intensity rather than financed emissions (different product scope/methodology). Using 2023 emissions data, financed emissions increased to 3,417 kt CO2e (Scopes 1–2, +537 kt) and 16,928 kt CO2e (Scope 3, +75 kt), driven by higher product drawdowns by some higher‑emitting clients. 2024 outstanding in scope ~€7.4 billion; CO2e intensity 19.1 kg CO2e/boe. Target: −24% vs 2022 by 2030; distance to 2030 IEA convergence metric 31%.
- Includes references to methodology and data sources: “Technical notes to the transition plan” and the “Financed emissions” table; cites IEA World Energy Outlook 2023. Visuals indicate convergence pathways versus the IEA NZE2050 scenario and ING’s 2030/2040 targets.

nodes.title: The key highlights of our action plan for oil & gas
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.2.1 The key highlights of our action plan for oil & gas
nodes.start_phrase: In March 2022, we announced we would stop dedicated financing to new oil & gas fields (upstream).
nodes.summary:
- Summarizes ING’s action plan for oil and gas in the 2024 Annual Report (Environment section), outlining a staged tightening of financing policies and a pivot to low‑carbon solutions.
- Policy timeline:
  - March 2022: Stopped dedicated financing for new upstream oil and gas fields.
  - March 2023: Extended restrictions to midstream infrastructure that enables new field developments.
  - December 2023: Announced phaseout of financing for upstream oil and gas activities by 2040.
  - September 2024: Decided to cease new financing for new LNG export terminals after 2025, aligned with IEA WEO 2023 NZE2050.
- Commits to reduce combined traded oil and gas volumes in line with IEA pathways and to include Trade and Commodity Finance in the Terra approach.
- Continues supporting clients transitioning to “new energies” that displace fossil hydrocarbons and help decarbonize other sectors.
- Details three focus areas for the hydrocarbons & new energies team:
  - Sustainable fuels (e-fuels and biofuels such as hydrogen, ammonia, biomethane, SAF) produced from non-fossil feedstocks.
  - Recycled feedstock for plastics via chemical recycling (e.g., pyrolysis) to replace fossil-based inputs.
  - Carbon capture and storage (industrial CO2 capture with storage in depleted gas fields or aquifers).
- Includes context of the broader report structure (strategy, governance, sustainability, risk, and financial statements).

nodes.title: Beyond our energy sector transition plan
nodes.heading: 4.1.7.3 Beyond our energy sector transition plan

nodes.summary:
- Outlines ING’s energy transition strategy with three headline commitments: end lending to individual coal‑fired power plants by 2025; phase out lending to clients with upstream oil & gas activities by 2040; and triple annual renewable power generation lending commitments to EUR 7.5 billion by 2025.
