The “Leave no one behind” strategy promotes inclusion for customers with and without disabilities. Emphasizes financial literacy to support informed decisions and financial health.

nodes.title: Customer strategy - Superior customer value
nodes.heading: 5.2.3 Customer strategy - Superior customer value
nodes.start_phrase: We strive to make banking easy, instant, personal and relevant so customers can stay up to date with all that ING offers.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and focus: Addresses consumers and end-users of ING’s services, prioritizing private individuals in Retail Banking per double materiality. Emphasis on fair access, transparent communication, and respect for customer rights.
- Vulnerable customers: Defines vulnerability (e.g., elderly; temporary/permanent sensory, physical, cognitive, neurodiverse disabilities; chronic disease; reading difficulties) and tailors care to prevent harm or exclusion.
- Key impacts and risks:
  - Access to quality information: Risks of unfair customer treatment and mis-selling leading to uninformed decisions and possible financial distress.
  - Social inclusion: Potential discrimination, accessibility barriers, regional restrictions, unequal treatment, and misleading marketing.
  - Privacy: Data protection risks under laws like GDPR, with potential identity theft, fraud, loss of privacy, and emotional distress.
  - Financial effects: Monitored via complaints and legal processes; no significant current financial effects reported for 2024.
- Customer engagement and accessibility:
  - Ongoing engagement led by the head of Retail; uses NPS and complaints to identify issues and improve services.
  - Global Centre of Expertise Accessibility participates in international forums, informs actions, supports EAA compliance, and co-published a 2024 report on EAA impacts (with Sia-Partners).
- Customer strategy – Superior customer value: Aims to make banking easy, instant, personal, and relevant; clear pricing and accessible communication; “Leave no one behind” accessibility strategy; promotes financial literacy; integrates privacy/data security and regulatory updates into risk and compliance frameworks.
- Governance and policy framework:
  - Customer Centricity Policy (CCP) rolled out globally in 2024 to prevent mis-selling/unfair treatment and ensure equitable access, including for persons with disabilities.
  - Integrates new regulations (e.g., European Accessibility Act, Consumer Credit Directive, Retail Investor Strategy) via governance measures, policy reviews, risk assessments, and control processes like the Product Approval and Review Process (PARP).
  - Sets minimum standards: act in customers’ and society’s interests; aligned complaint processes; clear, accessible, non-misleading information; suitability and needs assessment across the product lifecycle; consideration of ESG risks and customer impacts.
  - While no standalone customer human rights policy, seeks alignment through EU financial directives (e.g., IDD, MiFID). CCP to be enhanced in 2025 with minimum standards on non-discrimination and access to basic banking.
- Complaints and remediation:
  - CCP mandates transparent, accessible complaints processes across channels (assisted and self-service), regular assessment, and root-cause analysis.
  - Complaints can be filed via ING or third parties; anti-retaliation upheld via Whistleblower policy.
  - Resolution aims at first contact; escalations handled by specialized teams; outcomes can include product/process changes, compensation, and apologies; performance tracked via resolution timeliness and frequency to drive structural improvements.

nodes.title: Policies, actions and performance
nodes.heading: 5.2.4 Policies, actions and performance
nodes.start_phrase: ING offers a large variety of financial products and services to customers, and so we face different risks and are subject to a multitude of regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on customer-centric compliance and risk management covering non-discrimination, access to products and services, responsible marketing, and safeguarding customer privacy and data security.
- Continuous monitoring of regulatory developments and implementation through established governance to stay compliant while delivering superior customer value; processes integrated into existing risk and compliance frameworks.
- Reference to broader governance: human rights informing strategy and business model, and roles of the Management Board Banking detailed in the Sustainability Statement.
- Customer Centricity Policy (CCP):
  - Rolled out globally in 2024 to prevent and mitigate risks related to social inclusion, access to quality information, mis-selling, and unfair treatment.
  - Ensures equitable access, including for persons with disabilities; embeds governance to integrate regulations like the European Accessibility Act, Consumer Credit Directive, and Retail Investor Strategy.
  - Sets high-level obligations for product suitability across the customer lifecycle, fair pricing, clear and non-misleading communications, qualified advisory, and consideration of ESG risks and customer impacts.
  - Establishes global minimum standards: create/sell products in the interests of customers and society, aligned complaints processes, accessible information, and assessing individual customer needs at sale and during use to mitigate financial distress.
  - Alignment with human rights via relevant EU financial market directives (IDD, MiFID), with planned 2025 enhancements on accessibility, non-discrimination, and access to basic banking across all countries.
- Complaints and remediation:
  - Complaints used to identify impacts and drive structural improvements in products and processes.
  - Minimum requirements include transparent procedures, regular assessments, root-cause analyses, and keeping customers informed; customers can complain via third parties (distributors, brokers, manufacturers).
  - Multiple assisted and self-service channels are available and communicated through ING websites, terms and conditions, and customer support.
  - No tolerance for retaliation; protections referenced in the Whistleblower policy.
  - Handling model prioritizes resolution at first contact with escalation to specialized teams; performance measured by resolution time and frequency; remedies include product changes, financial compensation, and apologies.

nodes.title: Customer Centricity Policy
nodes.heading: 5.2.4.1 Customer Centricity Policy
nodes.start_phrase: ING offers a large variety of financial products and services to customers, and so we face different risks and are subject to a multitude of regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on customer-centric compliance covering non-discrimination, equitable access to products and services, responsible marketing, and strong privacy/data security, managed through ongoing regulatory monitoring and integrated risk/compliance processes.
- Human rights considerations inform strategy and business model; governance roles and responsibilities referenced in sustainability governance.
- Customer Centricity Policy (CCP) rolled out globally in 2024 to prevent mis-selling and unfair treatment and ensure accessible, suitable, and fairly priced products throughout the customer lifecycle.
- CCP embeds governance to implement evolving regulations (e.g., European Accessibility Act, Consumer Credit Directive, Retail Investor Strategy), with continuous policy reviews, risk assessments, and regulatory change management.
- Requirements include: clear, non-misleading product information; PARP oversight; trained professionals; consideration of ESG risks and impacts; global minimum standards on product suitability, standardized complaints handling, accessible information, and assessment of individual customer needs to reduce financial distress.
- Alignment with human rights through EU financial market directives (IDD, MiFID), with planned 2025 CCP enhancements to set minimum standards on accessibility, non-discrimination, and access to basic banking across all countries.
- Complaints and remediation framework: transparent, multi-channel access (assisted and self-service), progress updates, regular assessments and root-cause analyses, ability to complain via third parties, and no-retaliation protections via the whistleblower policy.
- Operational handling aims for first-contact resolution with escalation to specialized teams, monitoring of resolution times and rates, and remedies including product/process changes, financial compensation, and apologies, using complaint insights to drive structural improvements.

nodes.title: Complaints and remediation process
nodes.heading: 5.2.4.2 Complaints and remediation process
nodes.start_phrase: In addition to our general engagement activities, we use our complaints channels to gain a clearer picture of the impacts we have on our customers.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on customer-centric compliance and risk management integrated into existing frameworks, prioritizing non-discrimination, access to products and information, responsible marketing, and robust privacy/data security, with continuous regulatory monitoring.
- Governance context: human rights inform strategy and business model; oversight and roles addressed in sustainability governance.
- Customer Centricity Policy (CCP): rolled out globally in 2024; sets minimum standards for fair treatment, suitability, fair pricing, clear/non-misleading information, and aligned complaints processes; embeds ESG considerations and uses Product Approval and Review Process (PARP); governance to implement EU rules (European Accessibility Act, Consumer Credit Directive, Retail Investor Strategy); alignment with IDD/MiFID preambles in lieu of a dedicated customer human rights policy; planned 2025 enhancement to set minimum standards on accessibility, non-discrimination, and basic access to banking.
- Complaints and remediation: multi-channel access (assisted and self-service), transparency and status updates, regular assessments with root cause analysis, escalation to specialized teams, remedies (product changes, compensation, apologies), and structural improvements; anti-retaliation covered under Whistleblower policy; standardized complaint labels (human rights, accessibility, privacy, ESG, customer centricity) to go live in 2025 to improve root cause analysis and identify severe human rights incidents.
- Social inclusion and access to quality information: accessibility measures (voice-activated ATMs, notched cards, relay/sign-language services, accessible websites and apps with screen readers); EU-wide EAA compliance program targeted for completion in 2025; initiatives under UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking and the Commitment to Financial Health and Inclusion, including tools to build savings and manage expenses; monitoring of channel availability and service uptime; ongoing compliance monitoring, issue management, and periodic product reviews via PARP that may lead to remediation.
- Global Personal Data Protection Internal Policy (GPDP): GDPR-aligned policy governing lawful, purpose-limited, necessary, and accurate personal data processing; operational flows to fulfill data subject rights (access, erasure, objection, correction) timely; transparency on data use and sharing; ensuring equivalent protections with third parties and for cross-border transfers outside the EEA.

nodes.title: Actions regarding access to quality information and social inclusion
nodes.heading: 5.2.4.3 Actions regarding access to quality information and social inclusion
nodes.start_phrase: We have introduced various measures to make ING a more accessible bank, such as installing voice-activated ATMs in certain countries for people with a visual impairment to withdraw money, and issuing bank cards with a notch on top so they can insert them correctly.
nodes.summary:
- Customer complaints and human rights: Established channels and procedures for complaints; issues about complaint handling are addressed within broader customer concern evaluations. ING created standardized labels (human rights topics such as discrimination, accessibility, privacy; customer centricity; ESG) to tag complaints from 2025, enabling root-cause analysis, service remediation, customer journey improvements, potential human rights abuse identification and remedy, and stronger management oversight. A granular approach to identify severe human rights incidents is being developed.

- Social inclusion and access to information: Accessibility measures include voice-activated ATMs, notched bank cards, relay phone banking in Australia, sign-language services in Poland, and screen reader compatibility for Dutch web and mobile apps. A European Accessibility Act (EAA) program launched in 2022 aims for full compliance across EU retail operations by 2025. ING monitors and optimizes channel uptime, tracking availability through Channel Availability metrics.

- Financial health and inclusion: Collaboration with UNEP FI under the Principles for Responsible Banking to shape industry measurement of financial health. As a founding signatory of the Commitment to Financial Health and Inclusion, ING sets targets across products/services, data analytics, and partnerships. Tools promoting savings and expense management are deployed in multiple European locations.

- Compliance governance and product oversight: Customer Conduct Policy (CCP) is implemented across locations. Findings from monitoring, complaint and event analyses, and regulatory interactions are logged and tracked in a global issue database, with continuous, risk-based monitoring and periodic assessments. Product Approval and Review processes can trigger remediation if offerings are deemed unfit for customers.

- Data privacy and protection: A Global Personal Data Protection Internal Policy (GPDP), aligned with GDPR and other regulations, governs fair, lawful, purpose-specific processing with controls ensuring data necessity and accuracy. Operational processes support data subject rights (access, erasure, objection, correction) with timely handling per regulatory requirements. ING commits to transparency on data use and sharing and requires third parties, including those outside the EEA, to provide GDPR-equivalent protection.

nodes.title: Global Personal Data Protection Internal Policy
nodes.heading: 5.2.4.4 Global Personal Data Protection Internal Policy
nodes.start_phrase: Just as we strive to enable customers to engage with ING without issue or interruption, we aim to protect the information they provide to us throughout their ING journey.
nodes.summary:
- Complaints management: Established channels and procedures; customer confidence not separately measured but concerns are incorporated into broader evaluations. Outcomes from monitoring, complaints, events, and regulators are logged and tracked in a global database.

- Standardized complaint labels: In 2024 ING developed labels for human rights (e.g., discrimination, accessibility, privacy), customer centricity, and ESG; to go live in 2025 to enable root-cause analysis, remediation, improved customer journeys, senior management insights, and stronger customer trust. Work is underway to systematically identify severe human rights incidents.

- Accessibility and social inclusion: Accessibility measures include voice-activated ATMs, notched bank cards, relay service for phone banking in Australia, sign-language service in Poland, and screen-reader compatibility for Dutch web and mobile channels. An EU-wide program (EAA Program) is aligning customer-facing services with the European Accessibility Act by 2025. Continuous monitoring of channel uptime and availability supports uninterrupted access.

- Financial health and inclusion: Collaboration with UNEP FI under the Principles for Responsible Banking and as a founding signatory of the Commitment to Financial Health and Inclusion. Targets focus on products/services, data analytics, and partnerships. Tools have been implemented in multiple European markets to help customers build savings and manage expenses.

- Compliance and product governance: Compliance policies (including CCP) are implemented across locations with continuous, risk-based monitoring and periodic assessments. The Product Approval and Review Process (PARP) triggers remediation when products are deemed unfit.

- Data privacy governance (GPDP): A Global Personal Data Protection Internal Policy aligned with GDPR and other laws governs lawful, necessary, and accurate processing. Operational flows enable data subject rights (access, erasure, objection, etc.). Transparency on data use and third-country transfers is emphasized, with security aligned to current standards.

- Privacy risk management actions: Data Protection and Data Retention frameworks use DPIAs, Legitimate Interest Assessments, and Transfer Impact Assessments to identify and mitigate risks at process/IT-asset level and within PARP. Data breach response includes rapid containment, regulatory reporting where required, and lessons learned. Controls are monitored via Key Control Testing; governance and support provided by the Data Protection Executive Office and Data Protection Compliance. 2024 improvements focused on data retention and deletion.

- Metrics and targets: Channel Availability for Retail Banking is measured and disclosed for the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany. ING aims to minimize complaints/breaches related to access to information, inclusion, and data privacy, with internal monitoring via a Compliance Risk Framework and risk appetite indicators.

nodes.title: Actions regarding Privacy
nodes.heading: 5.2.4.5 Actions regarding Privacy
nodes.start_phrase: ING manages personal data protection and retention risks and impacts via the Global Data Protection and Data Retention frameworks and control standards.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines ING’s approach to managing personal data securely in line with information security standards, with further details in the Privacy Statement.
- Describes governance through Global Data Protection and Data Retention frameworks, supported by risk assessments:
  - Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) at processing-activity level
  - Legitimate Interest Assessment to balance ING’s interests with individuals’ rights
  - Transfer Impact Assessment for data transfers to non-EEA countries
- Explains that assessments drive concrete, granular mitigation measures embedded in new or changed business processes and documented at product level via the PARP process; policies and controls are continuously monitored and periodically assessed.
- Details incident response for personal data breaches, including rapid containment/mitigation, regulatory reporting where required, and lessons learned prioritizing customer impact.
- Notes periodic testing of data protection and retention controls via the Key Control Testing framework and clarifies roles of first- and second-line teams, the Data Protection Executive Office, and Data Protection Compliance; provides avenues for data protection complaints.
- Highlights 2024 improvements focused on data retention and deletion, and ongoing optimization to embed data protection requirements in business processes.
- Presents metrics and targets: monitoring of Retail Banking Channel Availability in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany; commitment to limit complaints/breaches related to information access, social inclusion, data privacy, and reputational risks; internal monitoring via a Compliance Risk Framework with risk appetite indicators.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 5.2.5 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: Regarding accessibility and availability of our channels, we monitor and report our Channel Availability for Retail Banking.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on ING’s management of personal data in line with information security standards, referencing the public Privacy Statement.
- Description of the Global Data Protection and Data Retention frameworks, policies, and control standards, including continuous monitoring and periodic assessment under a risk-based approach.
- Key risk assessment tools:
  - Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) at processing-activity level.
  - Legitimate Interest Assessment to balance ING’s interests with individuals’ rights.
  - Transfer Impact Assessment for transfers to non-EEA countries, evaluating contractual and technical safeguards.
- Embedding data protection into business and product lifecycles, including product-level assessments via the PARP process.
- Incident response for personal data security incidents (e.g., breaches): rapid containment and mitigation, regulatory reporting where required, and “lessons learned” to prevent recurrence with customer impact as a primary consideration.
- Ongoing control testing through the ING Key Control Testing framework and governance support by first and second lines, the Data Protection Executive Office, and Data Protection Compliance; guidance for process, asset, and contract owners; complaint channels described in the Privacy Statement.
- 2024 improvements centered on data retention and deletion, with continuous optimization to ensure compliant embedding of data protection requirements.
- Metrics and targets: monitoring Retail Banking channel availability (Netherlands, Belgium, Germany), limiting complaints/breaches related to information access, social inclusion, and data privacy, and overseeing reputational risks via the Compliance Risk Framework with risk appetite indicators.

nodes.title: Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 6.1.1 Identified impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: We have performed our double materiality assessment regarding business conduct on our own operations in the value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Defines business conduct as how ING conducts business, guided by the Global Code of Conduct, values, principles, and ethical standards, with a focus on anti-corruption, anti-bribery, and whistleblower protection.
- Double materiality assessment (covering ING’s own operations in the value chain) identified inherent risks of financial loss, regulatory fines, and reputational damage stemming from: breaches of corporate culture, bribery and corruption, and failure to protect whistleblowers.
- Mitigation through established policies and guidelines: Orange Code and Global Code of Conduct (corporate culture), Anti-Bribery and Corruption Policy and zero-tolerance statement (bribery/corruption), and Whistleblower Policy with supporting internal guidelines.
- Risk assessment and financial effects: evaluation based on ING’s internal risk database, workforce engagement, and whistleblower channels; accounting aligned with provisions and legal proceedings notes in the Financial Statements; no significant current financial effects reported for 2024.
- Governance and risk management: controls designed to identify and manage risks in a timely manner via a risk management cycle; acknowledgment of longer-term uncertainty due to evolving regulation and macro-social developments.
- Corporate culture emphasis: “integrity above all” via the Orange Code; the Global Code of Conduct links cultural values to detailed policies and rules.
- Business Conduct Framework components include (key policies in bold): Orange Code, Global Code of Conduct, Whistleblower Policy, Global Investigations Charter, Anti-Bribery and Corruption Policy (zero tolerance), ABC High-Risk Roles Guidance, and Global Event Management Procedure.

nodes.title: Policies, actions and performance
nodes.heading: 6.1.2 Policies, actions and performance
nodes.start_phrase: Our operations touch many lives: customers, employees, shareholders, and society at large.
nodes.summary:

nodes.title: Corporate Culture – Integrity above all
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.1 Corporate Culture – Integrity above all
nodes.start_phrase: Our operations touch many lives: customers, employees, shareholders, and society at large.
nodes.summary:
- Defines business conduct as how the company does business, anchored in the Global Code of Conduct and Orange Code, with a focus on corporate culture, anti-bribery and anti-corruption, and whistleblower protection as key sustainability matters.
- Double materiality assessment (own operations and value chain) identifies risks of financial loss, regulatory fines, and reputational damage arising from culture infringements, bribery/corruption, and failure to protect whistleblowers. Governance and risk management cycles are in place; longer-term uncertainty acknowledged due to evolving regulations. No significant current financial effects reported for 2024; financial impacts assessed via provisions and legal proceedings processes.
- Business Conduct Framework comprises core policies: Orange Code (integrity above all), Global Code of Conduct (linking values to rules), Anti-Bribery & Corruption Policy with a zero-tolerance stance, and Whistleblower Policy. Policies follow Internal Control Binding Principles, undergo annual compliance checks and periodic full reviews, and are accessible to staff; Orange Code and Global Code are public.
- Supporting processes and guidelines include: Global Investigations Charter (governance for investigations via Central Special Investigations), Global Event Management Procedure (operational risk event management), and ABC High-Risk Roles Guidance (identifying roles needing enhanced anti-bribery training). Mandatory global training covers the Code, whistleblowing, and anti-bribery/corruption.
- Orange Code details values (honest, prudent, responsible) and behaviors (take it on and make it happen; help others be successful; be a step ahead), embedded in performance standards.
- Risk culture is monitored via a methodology assessing maturity across entities on four behaviors: risk awareness, risk judgment, escalation and follow-up, and leadership. Insights draw from surveys, professional judgment, and quantitative indicators; progress tracked annually and discussed bi-annually by executive and supervisory bodies.
- Decision-making is supported by a four-step Orange Code model: define the dilemma; gather information and stakeholders; balance rights and interests; take and document the decision. In 2024, it was applied in areas such as environmental and social risk, product approval/review, data ethics, and model validation.
- Highlights the growing importance of behavioral risk—patterns in decision-making, communication, and ownership—as a driver of financial and non-financial risks, influenced by formal and informal mechanisms.

nodes.title: Corporate Culture – Integrity above all - Introduction
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.1 Corporate Culture – Integrity above all

nodes.title: The Orange Code
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.1.1 The Orange Code
nodes.start_phrase: The Orange Code describes what we can expect from each other when we turn up to work each day.
nodes.summary:
- Describes ING’s internal processes and guidelines that support global policies:
  - Global Investigations Charter: defines which incidents are handled by Central Special Investigations (CSI) and how investigations are initiated, conducted, and resolved; sets governing principles for the investigations function.
  - Global Event Management Procedure: outlines processes for managing operational risk events, mitigation responsibilities, and related reporting.
  - High-Risk Role Guidance: identifies roles vulnerable to bribery and corruption and sets criteria for High-Risk Role training.
- Emphasizes mandatory global training to embed business conduct policies (Global Code of Conduct, whistleblower, anti-bribery and corruption).
- Explains the Orange Code (ING’s shared culture since 2014):
  - Values: We are honest, prudent, responsible.
  - Behaviours: You take it on and make it happen; You help others be successful; You are always a step ahead.
  - Embedded in mutual commitments and performance standards.
- Details risk culture approach:
  - Monitors maturity across entities via a methodology focused on four behaviours: risk awareness, risk judgement, escalation & follow-up, leadership.
  - Uses multiple inputs (annual survey, professional judgement, quantitative indicators).
  - Progress tracked annually; discussed bi-annually by the MBB and Supervisory Board.
- Outlines the Orange Code decision-making model for dilemmas:
  - Steps: define the issue/options; gather information and stakeholders; balance rights and interests; take and document the decision (including damage control).
  - 2024 focus on supporting decision and advisory bodies (e.g., environmental and social risk, product approval/review, data ethics, model validation) with structured dilemma dialogues.
- Introduces behavioural risk:
  - Recognizes its growing importance and intangibility.
  - Arises from patterns in decision-making, communication, and ownership.
  - Driven by both formal and informal mechanisms, affecting financial and non-financial risks.

nodes.title: Behavioural risk
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.1.4 Behavioural risk
nodes.start_phrase: Behavioural risk is an increasingly important area for ING and across the financial industry.
nodes.summary:
- Describes ING’s internal processes and guidelines that complement global policies, including:
  - Global Investigations Charter: defines incidents under Central Special Investigations (CSI) or local responsibility and sets principles for independent, objective, confidential investigations.
  - Global Event Management Procedure: governs management, mitigation, and reporting of operational risk events.
  - High-Risk Role Guidance: identifies roles vulnerable to bribery and corruption to target High-Risk Role training.
- Highlights global mandatory training and awareness for conduct-related policies (Code of Conduct, whistleblowing, anti-bribery & corruption), with onboarding and annual acknowledgements monitored via the compliance risk dashboard.
- Explains the Orange Code as ING’s cultural foundation, outlining values (honest, prudent, responsible) and behaviors (take it on and make it happen; help others be successful; be a step ahead), embedded in performance expectations.
- Details risk culture monitoring: a methodology assessing maturity across entities on risk awareness, risk judgment, escalation and follow-up, and leadership, using surveys, professional judgment, and indicators; progress tracked annually with bi-annual MBB and Supervisory Board discussions.
- Presents the Orange Code decision-making model (define dilemma; gather information and stakeholders; balance rights and interests; decide and document), with 2024 focus on embedding dilemma dialogues in bodies handling E&S risk, product approvals/reviews, data ethics, and model validation.
- Covers behavioral risk management: nature and drivers (formal governance/processes and informal dynamics/beliefs); behavioral risk assessments targeting group effectiveness, leadership, team dynamics, and unwritten norms; evidence-based interventions. Notes a 2024 global activation to strengthen productive conversations and improve speak-up and escalation, starting with senior leadership and supported by e-learning/toolkits.
- Summarizes the Global Code of Conduct: 10 conduct principles grounded in the Orange Code (including AB&C and whistleblowing), required e-learning at onboarding and annual acknowledgement; updated in 2024 with a new mandatory global learning launching Q1 2025 and supporting communications.
- Details the Whistleblower Policy: multiple internal speak-up channels, anonymous reporting option, strict confidentiality and anti-retaliation; external reporting via ing.com. Describes standardized intake/scoping by Whistleblower Reporting Officers and investigations by CSI or local SIF under the Investigations Charter. Notes 2024 enhancements to protect reporters, revamped global/specialist learnings, local annexes to meet EU Directive 2019/1937 requirements, a new global e-learning and specialist learning journey for officers, and monitoring of completion via the compliance risk dashboard alongside a global support community.

nodes.title: Behavioural risk - Introduction
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.1.4 Behavioural risk
nodes.start_phrase: Behavioural risk is an increasingly important area for ING and across the financial industry.
nodes.summary: This Governance section of the ING Group Annual Report 2024 introduces behavioural risk as a growing focus for ING and the financial industry, defining it as risk arising when behavioural patterns underpin financial and non-financial risks. It emphasizes the intangibility and complexity of assessing behaviour, focusing on patterns in decision-making, communication, and willingness to take ownership. The text distinguishes formal drivers (e.g., organisational processes and governance structure) from informal drivers (e.g., group dynamics and underlying beliefs) that shape behaviour.

nodes.title: Behavioural risk assessments
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.1.4.1 Behavioural risk assessments
nodes.start_phrase: Behavioural risk assessments identify and analyse undesired behaviours within ING and provide management with specific direction on how to change these behaviours.
nodes.summary:
- Defines risk culture drivers: formal (processes, governance) and informal (group dynamics, underlying beliefs).
- Behavioural risk assessments: identify undesired group behaviours, leadership influence, team dynamics and unwritten norms; use a framework to target areas needing deeper investigation and provide management with actionable guidance.
- Behavioural risk interventions: evidence-based measures designed using behavioural and organisational science; 2024 global activation plan to promote productive conversations, speak-up and escalation, starting with senior leadership and supported by e-learning and a toolkit for wider rollout.
- Global Code of Conduct: builds on the Orange Code and sets 10 conduct principles, including anti-bribery & corruption and whistleblowing; mandatory onboarding training and annual attestations monitored via the compliance risk dashboard; updated in 2024 with a new mandatory global learning scheduled for Q1 2025 and supporting communications.
- Whistleblower Policy: multiple speak-up channels (managers, HR, confidential advisers, Whistleblower Reporting Officers) including anonymous reporting; strict anti-retaliation stance; external parties can report via ing.com; concerns tracked and scoped by Whistleblower Reporting Officers, with investigations by Corporate Special Investigations or local Special Investigations Functions under the Global Investigations Charter to ensure independence, objectivity, impartiality, and confidentiality.
- 2024 enhancements: reinforced protections for reporters; updated global policy and procedures; revamped global and specialist trainings; local policy annexes aligned to national transpositions of EU Directive 2019/1937; new mandatory e-learning on whistleblowing (rights, anonymity, confidentiality, retaliation awareness, follow-up) with completion monitored via the compliance risk dashboard; launch of a specialist learning journey and resources for Reporting Officers.

nodes.title: Behavioural risk interventions
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.1.4.2 Behavioural risk interventions
nodes.start_phrase: Based on the results of the executed behavioural risk assessments, interventions are taken to mitigate the behavioural risks in a focused manner.
nodes.summary:
- Defines formal drivers (processes, governance) and informal drivers (group dynamics, beliefs) that shape behaviour at ING.
- Describes behavioural risk assessments focused on groups, leadership, team dynamics, and social norms to identify and understand drivers of undesired behaviours, guided by a behavioural risk management framework.
- Outlines behavioural risk interventions based on assessment results, using behavioural and organisational science to design targeted mitigations.
- Highlights a 2024 global activation to promote productive conversations and strengthen speak-up and escalation behaviours, launched with senior leadership, supported by e-learning and a toolkit for broader rollout.
- Summarises ING’s Global Code of Conduct: 10 conduct principles (including anti-bribery & corruption and whistleblowing), mandatory onboarding e-learning, annual adherence acknowledgment monitored via the compliance risk dashboard, and a 2024 update with a new global required learning launching in Q1 2025.
- Details the Whistleblower Policy: multiple speak-up channels (managers, HR, confidential advisers, Whistleblower Reporting Officers), anonymous reporting, strict confidentiality, and zero tolerance for retaliation; external stakeholders can also report via ING’s website.
- Explains the follow-up process: concerns are scoped and reviewed by Whistleblower Reporting Officers; investigations are conducted by Corporate Special Investigations (CSI) or local Special Investigations Functions (SIF) under the Global Investigations Charter to ensure independence, objectivity, and confidentiality.
- Notes 2024 enhancements: updated global policy and procedures strengthening reporter protections, revamped global and specialist trainings, and local policy annexes aligned with national transpositions of EU Directive 2019/1937.
- Reports rollout of a mandatory global e-learning on whistleblowing (rights, anonymity, confidentiality, anti-retaliation, follow-up), with completion monitored via the compliance risk dashboard, and a new specialist learning journey for Whistleblower Reporting Officers with guidance and templates.
- Context: excerpt appears in the Governance section of the ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: ING’s Global Code of Conduct
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.2 ING’s Global Code of Conduct
nodes.start_phrase: Building on the values and behaviours of our Orange Code, the ING Global Code of Conduct outlines the 10 conduct principles expected from all of us.
nodes.summary:
- Defines conduct drivers: formal (processes, governance) and informal (group dynamics, beliefs).
- Describes behavioural risk management: assessments that analyze group effectiveness, leadership, team dynamics, and unwritten norms to identify undesired behaviours; a framework guides identification of risks needing deeper review.
- Details behavioural risk interventions: evidence-based, targeted mitigations informed by assessments. In 2024 a global activation promoted productive conversations and improved speak‑up/escalation, starting with senior leadership and supported by e-learning and a toolkit for wider rollout.
- Outlines ING’s Global Code of Conduct: 10 conduct principles grounded in the Orange Code, including anti-bribery & corruption and whistleblowing policies. Employees complete onboarding e-learning and annually acknowledge adherence; acknowledgements are monitored via the compliance risk dashboard. The Code was updated in 2024, with a mandatory global learning slated for Q1 2025 and accompanying communications.
- Summarizes the Whistleblower Policy: multiple internal speak‑up channels (managers, HR, confidential advisers, Whistleblower Reporting Officers), anonymous reporting option, strict confidentiality, and zero tolerance for retaliation. External stakeholders can report via ing.com.
- Explains whistleblowing governance and process: concerns tracked by Whistleblower Reporting Officers through intake/scoping and review; investigations conducted by Corporate Special Investigations (CSI) or local Special Investigations Functions (SIF) under the Global Investigations Charter to ensure independence, objectivity, impartiality, and confidentiality.
- Notes 2024 enhancements: updated policy and global procedure reinforcing reporter protection; revamped global and specialist trainings; local policy annexes aligned with EU Directive 2019/1937; new mandatory e-learning on whistleblowing (rights, anonymity, confidentiality, anti-retaliation, follow-up) with completion monitored; expanded support community and a specialist learning journey with obligations, interviewing guidance, and templates.
- Context: Extract from the Governance section of ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Whistleblower Policy
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.3 Whistleblower Policy
nodes.start_phrase: At ING we systematically look for ways to enhance and harmonise our ‘speak up’ channels.
nodes.summary:
- Defines behavioural drivers of conduct risk at ING: formal drivers (processes, governance) and informal drivers (group dynamics, beliefs).
- Describes behavioural risk assessments that analyse undesired group behaviours, leadership influence, team dynamics and unwritten norms, using a firm-wide framework to identify areas needing deeper review.
- Outlines behavioural risk interventions based on assessment insights, using behavioural and organisational science; highlights a 2024 global activation to promote productive conversations and strengthen speak-up/escalation, starting with senior leadership and supported by e-learning and toolkits for broader rollout.
- Summarises ING’s Global Code of Conduct: 10 conduct principles aligned with the Orange Code, including anti-bribery & corruption and whistleblowing; mandatory onboarding e-learning and annual adherence acknowledgment tracked via the compliance risk dashboard; updated in 2024 with a new required global learning launching in Q1 2025.
- Details the Whistleblower Policy: multiple internal channels (managers, HR, confidential advisers, Whistleblower Reporting Officers), anonymous reporting, strict confidentiality, and zero tolerance for retaliation; external stakeholders can report via the “Complaints about our conduct” page.
- Explains case handling: concerns logged by Whistleblower Reporting Officers, scoped and reviewed; investigations conducted by Corporate Special Investigations or local Special Investigations Functions under the Global Investigations Charter to ensure independence, objectivity, impartiality and confidentiality.
- Notes 2024 enhancements: updated global policy and procedure reinforcing reporter protection, revamped global and specialist trainings, local annexes to meet EU Directive 2019/1937 requirements, a new mandatory whistleblowing e-learning with completion monitored via the compliance risk dashboard, and a specialist learning journey and community to support Reporting Officers.
- Places the content within the Governance section of the ING Group Annual Report 2024.

nodes.title: Anti-bribery and Corruption Policy
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.4 Anti-bribery and Corruption Policy
nodes.start_phrase: We are committed to doing business in an honest, prudent and responsible manner and aim to ensure compliance with applicable anti-bribery and corruption (AB&C) laws and regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines ING’s Anti-Bribery & Corruption (AB&C) Policy, emphasizing a zero‑tolerance stance toward bribery, improper inducements, and corruption across all relationships, with the same expectations for partners and third parties.
- Describes governance: CSI leads independent, objective, and confidential investigations; all entities must report incidents via the Global Event Management Procedure to the Management Board and the chairman of the Supervisory Board.
- Details risk monitoring: a monthly key risk indicator tracks zero tolerance to bribery/corruption by employees and third parties, using event data from the iRisk Non‑Financial Risk tool; reports are not externally validated.
- Notes 2024 outcomes: no convictions or fines for AB&C violations; no related provisions recorded.
- Announces an updated AB&C Policy effective 1 April 2024, aligned with laws including the US FCPA and UK Bribery Act; published internally and on ing.com.
- Covers training: global mandatory AB&C training for all employees/contractors (part of financial crime fundamentals) to recognize risks, understand impacts, manage/mitigate risks, and escalate concerns; ongoing since Q1 2023 and required for new joiners.
- Explains High-Risk Roles (HRR): roles with elevated AB&C exposure identified via HRR Guidance; 2024 HRR e‑learning (~1 hour) covers regulatory requirements and breach impact, internal AB&C governance and controls, gifts & entertainment processes, public official risks, hiring risks, and third‑party engagement risks.
- Reports training completion: 98% completion for global mandatory training; 89% for eligible HRR training; monitored via a compliance dashboard.
- Notes that in 2024 the management and Supervisory Boards did not receive targeted AB&C training (board education information referenced elsewhere).
